title: Cells and Genetics
summary: Learn the biology of cells and inheritance: cell structure and microscopes, diffusion, osmosis and active transport, mitosis and meiosis, DNA and protein synthesis, Punnett squares and sickle-cell inheritance, and genetics in health and society.
audience: Secondary and first-year students, health learners and anyone curious about biology

body.p: All living things are made of cells, the basic units of life. Some organisms, such as bacteria, are single cells; humans have tens of trillions of cells of hundreds of types.

list: Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) are small and simple, with no nucleus; their DNA floats in the cytoplasm.
Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi) are larger, with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Nucleus: contains DNA and controls the cell.
Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves.
Cytoplasm: where many reactions happen.
Mitochondria: release energy by respiration.
Ribosomes: make proteins.
Plant cells also have a cell wall (cellulose, for support), chloroplasts (for photosynthesis) and a large permanent vacuole.

body.p: Magnification = image size / actual size. A cell drawn 15 mm wide that is really 0.05 mm wide has been magnified 15 / 0.05 = 300 times. A light microscope with a 10x eyepiece and 40x objective magnifies 400 times; electron microscopes reveal much finer detail.

body.tip: Convert both sizes to the same unit before calculating magnification.

lessons.title: Movement in and out of cells

body.p: Cells must take in substances (oxygen, glucose, water) and remove wastes (carbon dioxide, urea).

list: Diffusion: particles spread from high to low concentration, needing no energy; oxygen diffuses from the lungs into the blood.

Osmosis: water moves across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. Plant cells in salty water lose water and wilt; this is why over-fertilised or salty soils harm crops.
Active transport: cells use energy to move substances against a concentration gradient, as root hairs absorb minerals from soil.

body.p: Respiration releases energy from glucose in every living cell: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). Photosynthesis in plant chloroplasts uses light energy: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Together they cycle carbon and oxygen through living things.

body.tip: Remember osmosis as diffusion of water: water moves to where there is relatively less of it.

body.p: Cells reproduce by dividing. DNA is packaged into chromosomes; human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent.

list: Mitosis produces two genetically identical cells with the full 46 chromosomes. It is used for growth, repair and replacing cells, such as healing skin.
Meiosis produces four genetically different sex cells (gametes: sperm and eggs) with half the number, 23 chromosomes. Fertilisation restores 46.
Variation arises because meiosis shuffles chromosomes and swaps sections, and because each child gets a random combination from two parents.

body.p: Cancer occurs when cells divide uncontrollably because of mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle. Risk factors include tobacco, some infections (such as human papillomavirus, preventable with vaccination), radiation and age. Screening and early detection save lives.

body.tip: Mitosis makes two identical body cells; meiosis makes four varied sex cells with half the chromosomes.

body.p: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) carries genetic information. It is a double helix of two strands built from four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).
A always pairs with T, and C with G. So if 30% of the bases in a DNA sample are A, 30% are T, leaving 40% shared equally: 20% C and 20% G.

list: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein.
Transcription: the gene is copied into messenger RNA.
Translation: ribosomes read the RNA in groups of three bases (codons) and join amino acids into a protein.
Proteins build structures (such as collagen) and do jobs (such as enzymes and hemoglobin).

body.p: A mutation is a change in DNA. Most have little effect; some are harmful; a few are beneficial. Sickle-cell disease results from a single base change in the gene for hemoglobin.

body.tip: Remember base pairing with "Apple in the Tree, Car in the Garage": A-T, C-G.

body.p: Genes come in different versions called alleles. You inherit one allele of each gene from each parent.

list: Dominant alleles (written with a capital letter, A) show their effect even with one copy.
Recessive alleles (a) show only when two copies are present (aa).
Genotype: the alleles present (AA, Aa or aa). Phenotype: the observable characteristic.
Homozygous: two identical alleles; heterozygous: two different alleles.

body.p: Crossing two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) gives offspring AA, Aa, Aa and aa: a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio and a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio, so each child has a 25% chance of being aa. Crossing Aa with aa gives 50% Aa and 50% aa.

Sickle-cell disease follows recessive inheritance. If two parents each carry the trait (AS), each child has a 25% chance of sickle-cell disease (SS), a 50% chance of being a carrier (AS) and a 25% chance of AA. Carriers have some protection against severe malaria, which is why the allele is common in parts of Africa.

body.tip: Probabilities apply to each child separately; having one affected child does not change the chance for the next.

list: Genetic screening and counselling help families understand risks, for example newborn screening and pre-marital sickle-cell testing.
DNA profiling identifies individuals in forensic cases and paternity disputes.
Genetically modified crops, such as insect-resistant or drought-tolerant varieties, aim to raise yields; debates concern safety, biodiversity, costs and farmers' rights.
Gene therapy and gene editing (such as CRISPR) offer possible treatments, including for sickle-cell disease.
Genomic research on African populations, which hold the greatest human genetic diversity, can improve medicine for everyone.

body.p: Who owns genetic data? Can insurers or employers use it? How should consent work for research on communities? Should we edit genes that are passed to future generations? Genetic information is sensitive personal data and must be protected under data-protection laws, and research should benefit the communities who take part.

body.tip: When you read a headline about "a gene for" something, remember that most traits involve many genes and the environment together.
